finding: The live range of $100-$440 is too wide for one job because it mixes two: a belt alone and a belt with its tensioner. For a belt alone the bottom is about right and the top is too high; the top only fits when the tensioner is replaced as well, and a dealer-priced tensioner can pass it. Built totals for the belt alone (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $61-$207 (0.3-1.0 hr); midsize 2016 Camry about $82-$196 (0.4-1.0 hr); truck 2016 Tacoma 3.5L about $73-$246 (0.2-1.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $141-$271 (1.0-1.5 hr). The low ends pair an online belt price with a manufacturer warranty time of 12 to 24 minutes, which is less than most shops will bill for any visit; the four benchmarks start at $109-$154, so $100 is a fair floor. Nothing built or benchmarked for a belt alone passes about $300. If a job runs to the 1.5 hours one parts retailer's guide mentions for hard-to-reach belts, add about $60-$80 to the mainstream tops. Belt plus tensioner: the only stated time found for both together is a Chrysler bulletin (TSB 09-004-23, 2022 Pacifica Hybrid 3.6L), 0.9 hr to inspect and replace the tensioner and serpentine belt; a Ram bulletin (09-008-20, 2020 Ram 1500 3.6L eTorque) allows 0.6 hr to inspect and replace that engine's hydraulic belt tensioner alone. Neither is one of the example vehicles. Using 0.9 hr: Camry with an aftermarket belt-and-tensioner kit ($69.95) about $178; BMW 328i about $174 with an OE-supplier tensioner and aftermarket belt ($65.95) and about $335 with genuine parts at list ($191.01); Corolla with a genuine tensioner and belt at list ($357.59) about $466-$502. So about $175-$500 covers belt plus tensioner, and a split into roughly $100-$300 for the belt alone and $175-$500 with the tensioner would serve a reader better than one $100-$440 range. How solid the labor times are: only the truck low end is for the example vehicle (Toyota's own 0.2 hr for the Tacoma). The economy low end is a Hyundai campaign time for a 2018 Elantra; the midsize low end is a mechanic's guide quoting 0.4 hr for an Accord and 0.6 hr for an Altima, with model years not shown; every high end is a general statement that a belt takes about an hour. No stated time was found for any BMW, so the luxury class rests on general guides alone (1.0-1.5 hr), and no tensioner time was found for the Corolla, Camry, Tacoma or 328i. The Tacoma is a midsize pickup; GM's 0.4 hr for a 2017 Silverado HD diesel suggests full-size trucks are in the same range, but no full-size truck parts were priced. No fitment-confirmed aftermarket tensioner price was found for the Corolla or Tacoma. This is an estimate, not a quote.
extras: A quote often adds the belt tensioner (parts seen here: $44.67 OE-supplier to $159.77 genuine for the BMW; $311.03 list for a genuine Corolla tensioner; a Camry belt-and-tensioner kit at $69.95) and its labor, bringing the job to about $175-$500. Idler pulleys are often quoted at the same time; one retailer's guide says worn tensioners or idler pulleys add $80-$300. Also possible: a diagnosis fee for a squeal or chirp, shop supplies and sales tax. A belt soaked by a coolant or oil leak means the leak is quoted separately, and a failing water pump, alternator or A/C compressor pulley found during the job is a separate repair. Some engines use a second belt or a stretch-fit belt that needs a special tool.
